extracted.intended_audience: marketing/advertising researchers, grant reviewers, and academic evaluators
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for designing, conducting, and evaluating empirical research in advertising, marketing communications, and consumer behavior (as exemplified by A.A.A.A.-funded projects). Emphasis on theory linkage, measurement, sample design, statistical analysis, and practical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical framework / relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should be grounded in a clear theoretical framework (e.g., Hulett's two-way, transactional model of human communication) that links constructs (e.g., empathy/social acuity) to expected communication outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how the study's hypotheses and measures derive from and test the chosen theory; highlight uniqueness or novelty (this Auer grant was unique in testing communicators' empathic skills tied to Hulett's model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis specification (null form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses should be stated in testable form (the report notes Dr. Auer's research hypothesis tested in null form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state null and alternative hypotheses so statistical tests are interpretable; ensure directional vs nondirectional choice matches theory and analysis (page reports one-tailed and two-tailed tests explicitly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of validated measurement instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ measurement tests with documented psychometric properties (e.g., Guilford tests, Johnson's 'Judgment of Interests'), using instruments that have undergone validity and reliability evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer established instruments; if using newer instruments, report their development, normative data, prior sample means/SDs, and any invitations for further testing (Johnson invited further testing of his instrument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions checked and normative comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: When using published normative data and test statistics, check distributional assumptions (e.g., normality) and validate assumptions with qualified experts when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply appropriate scaling techniques if data depart from normality; document consultations or approvals (the study checked assumptions with Dr. Nancy Wiggins who approved them). Use normative means and SDs explicitly when comparing samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample composition and adequate sample size
rubrics_metrics.description: Design sampling to include relevant professional samples and comparison groups (e.g., 464 agency professionals, 434 college students, 59 high school students) and report sampling frame (agencies, cities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include appropriate comparison baselines and sufficient N to detect expected effects; describe sub-samples (e.g., account personnel) and report subgroup analyses where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical significance reporting and appropriate tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Report levels of statistical significance and specify test directionality (e.g., .001 level one-tailed, .001 two-tailed, .05 two-tailed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose one- vs two-tailed tests consistent with hypotheses; report exact p-levels and interpret results relative to population norms or comparison samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity and reliability testing of new instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: If developing new measuring instruments, subject them to validity and reliability testing before field use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document development procedures, validation samples, and reliability estimates; use validated instruments for field studies and dissertations (the report notes instruments were subjected to validity and reliability testing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitudinal panel data for sequential/hierarchy hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use longitudinal panels to observe consumers over time to test sequential assumptions (e.g., hierarchy of effects: beliefs → attitudes → intentions → purchase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect repeated measures under natural conditions (the MRCA panel of 182 housewives is cited); longitudinal design allows testing of causal/temporal sequence hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of moderators and multi-variable predictors
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess potential moderator variables (e.g., involvement, confidence) and compare the predictive power of the focal measure (e.g., Fishbein attitude score) against other commonly used predictors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate which variables limit or moderate attitude–behavior relationships; compare multiple predictors rather than relying on a single measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction effects and combined-variable analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate combined effects and interactions between message-bound and audience-bound factors rather than treating explanatory variables in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use methods that detect interactions (e.g., AID, MCA) and construct complex explanatory variables (e.g., lifestyle) when appropriate; interpret how interacting variables jointly predict behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate and innovative analytic techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply suitable statistical/computer techniques for the research question (the report cites AID and MCA used in tandem as methodological innovation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select analytic tools that can empirically determine which variable combinations best distinguish behavior levels; justify methodological innovations and explain their utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cluster analysis and segmentation validity
rubrics_metrics.description: When segmenting markets, define segments using purchase sequences or behavior and then differentiate segments by demographics and socioeconomic variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clustering methods to define actionable segments (consumer-product-marketing activity 'typology'); validate segments across product classes and examine implications for strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizability and cautious inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about generalizing findings beyond the studied product/category/context (the report warns that findings may not generalize beyond the product studied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state limits to generalizability, consider product-related factors (salience, familiarity), and avoid overextending conclusions from a single product category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed-methods supplementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplement quantitative models with qualitative or case-study data (e.g., interviews with executives) to enrich interpretation and predictive capability (Lens Model example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine quantitative model data with interviews/case studies to capture decision criteria not evident from quantitative approaches alone; use mixed methods when studying complex managerial decisions or transferability across markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical implications for practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should yield practical recommendations for advertisers (e.g., timing/content of advertising, role of media, segmentation strategy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate empirical findings into actionable guidance (e.g., adjust timing/content because rapid turnover of information seekers; use multiple media to play complementary roles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey/question wording effects (aided vs unaided recall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey methodology choices (aided vs unaided recall, question types, ranking criteria) materially affect measured responses about information source importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and justify the type of recall and ranking procedure; compare methods and interpret discrepancies cautiously rather than accepting one method's results uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for adequate data to estimate model parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical models of advertising effect and budget optimization require sufficient and appropriate data to estimate parameters and to test relative validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek cooperative industry partners for data when needed; document limitations if available data are insufficient to estimate parameters or test models fully (report cites insufficient data from cooperating advertisers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative analysis of practitioner vs academic perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe and analyze differences between how practitioners and academics view the communications process and research utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight areas where practitioners seek specific, immediate applications while academics prioritize generalizable models; propose ways the two disciplines might interact more meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documenting methodological innovations and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing methodological innovations or new measures, document their development, limitations, and current status (in progress, preliminary results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both promising avenues and incomplete results; identify next steps (e.g., further data collection, instrument refinement) so readers and funders understand the research trajectory.
